summary: Provides guidance for IANA when assigning parameters for fields in the IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, UDP and TCP headers. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: This is a rulebook for the person who hands out numbers for the fields in network messages.

questions: how does iana assign ip header values
iana allocation guidelines for ip headers
how does iana assign tcp and udp ports
subtitle: Writes down which approval process IANA follows when handing out values in IP, ICMP, UDP and TCP header fields.

tldr.problem: IANA had long assigned values for fields in older protocols such as IP, ICMP, UDP and TCP, but the rules for doing so had never been consistently written down.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2780 codifies existing IANA practice, field by field, by naming the process (such as Standards Action, IESG Approval or Expert Review) required to allocate each kind of value.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that gives IANA a fixed reference for these headers, and it has been updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 2780 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 37) and has not been obsoleted. It has been updated by RFC 4443, RFC 5237, RFC 5771, RFC 6335 and RFC 7045.

sections.title: Why the Rules Were Written Down
sections.content:
The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) has long allocated parameter values for fields in protocols created or maintained by the IETF. Starting a few years before this memo, the IETF began giving IANA guidance for new protocols, but guidance was not consistently provided for protocols developed before 1998.

RFC 2780 codifies existing IANA practice for the fields in the IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, UDP and TCP headers for which IANA assigns values. It expects further memos for other cases. It uses the process names from RFC 2434: Specification Required, Expert Review, IESG Approval, IETF Consensus and Standards Action.

Temporary assignments for experiments are made from time to time, and they require IESG Approval.
sections.eli5: The locker-number person already had habits, but nobody had written them down. This note writes them down.

sections.title: IPv4 Header Fields
sections.content:
The Version field is the first field of the IP header. New values define new versions of IP and are allocated only after an IETF Standards Action. Some Version bits are used by header compression schemes, so this matters in practice. For IPv4 the Version field is always 4.

The old Type of Service field has been superseded by the 6-bit Differentiated Services (DS) field and a 2-bit field that is currently reserved. DS values follow the IANA considerations in RFC 2474. Experimental uses of the 2-bit field may be assigned after IESG Approval, and permanent values need a Standards Action.

The Protocol field is allocated by Expert Review, IESG Approval or Standards Action. Expert Review should be used only in special cases involving non-disclosure information. The Option Type field is allocated by IESG Approval, IETF Consensus or Standards Action.

For addresses, unicast space is delegated to ICANN guidelines, except 0/8 and 127/8, where further assignments need a Standards Action because current implementations may break. Multicast addresses from 224.0.0.0 to 224.0.0.255 are reserved for routing and other low-level protocols, and new values there need IESG Approval or Standards Action. Addresses from 240.0.0.0 through 255.255.255.254 are reserved and are not to be assigned unless a Standards Action makes them valid.
sections.eli5: Some numbers are easy to hand out, like a visitor badge. Others, like the ones the whole school depends on, need the principal's agreement first.

sections.title: IPv6 Header Fields
sections.content:
The IPv6 Version field is always 6. The Traffic Class field is treated like the IPv4 DS field, with a 6-bit DS field and a 2-bit reserved field, and follows the same rules. The Next Header field shares its name space with the IPv4 Protocol field, so it is allocated the same way.

For addresses, the IAB gave IANA responsibility for all IPv6 address space. IANA agreed to guidelines formulated by the Regional Internet Registries for the Aggregatable Global Unicast format prefix (FP 001). Anycast addresses come out of the unicast space and cannot be told apart from unicast addresses. Multicast addresses are identified by a format prefix of 0xFF. Unassigned and reserved format prefixes need IESG Approval or Standards Action.

Hop-by-Hop and Destination Options values are allocated by IESG Approval, IETF Consensus or Standards Action. The Neighbor Discovery Type, Code and Option Type fields need IESG Approval or Standards Action.
sections.eli5: IPv6 has its own set of lockers, and most of them follow the same rules as the old ones, with a few special rows for special visitors.

sections.title: ICMP, UDP and TCP Fields
sections.content:
For ICMP (both the IPv4 and IPv6 versions), new Type values are allocated by IESG Approval or Standards Action. Code values for existing Types use the same processes. The policy for Code values of a new Type should be defined in the document that defines the Type.

UDP and TCP source and destination ports share one name space per protocol. Values are assigned by Specification Required, Expert Review, IESG Approval, IETF Consensus or Standards Action, and some assignments may involve non-disclosure information.

The reserved bits in the TCP header are assigned only by Standards Action, and values in the TCP Option Kind field need IESG Approval or Standards Action.
sections.eli5: Port numbers are like apartment numbers for programs. A few different groups of people can approve a new one, and the rules for the secret bits are stricter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Firewalls and intrusion detection monitors often rely on unambiguous interpretations of these header fields. When new values are assigned, an existing analyzer that does not understand them may fail in one of two ways. It may decline to forward the unrecognized traffic and cause loss of connectivity, or it may forward it and cause loss of security if the new values are used in an attack.

The memo argues that this vulnerability favors high visibility for assignments whenever possible, which the Standards Action and IETF Consensus processes ensure.
sections.eli5: Security guards at the gate know the list of badges. If a new badge appears without warning, they might turn away a friend or let in the wrong person, so new badges should be announced loudly.
